interactive.title: What percentage is it?
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on a percentage bar, the whole lined up with 100% and the amounts underneath, some showing an idea and the rest asking you to try it.
interactive.ignores: The amounts are example values, chosen to show the rule.

explain.text:
To say what percentage one amount is of another, line the whole up with 100%. The part then fills part ÷ whole of it, a share written as a decimal. Per cent means out of 100, and to change a decimal to a percentage you multiply by 100.[^1] So for a 9 V drop on 230 V, 9 ÷ 230 is about 0.039, which times 100 is 3.9%. As a check, 1% of 230 V is 2.3 V, and 9 V is just under four of those.

Keep the part on top. 230 ÷ 9 answers a different question, how many 9 V pieces fit in 230 V. A part smaller than its whole comes to under 100%, and a part bigger than its whole comes to over 100%, so 25 A on a 20 A rating is 125%. The whole is whatever the question compares with. Power lost is compared with the power put in, not the power that comes out, and 47 Ω off a resistor marked 470 Ω is compared with the 470 Ω, which makes 10%.[^2][^3]

**Divide the part by the whole and times by 100. The whole is 100%, the part goes on top, and 1% of the whole is a quick check.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** Divide the part by the whole, then times by 100.[^1] The whole is the amount the question compares with, and it goes underneath.

**Worked example:** A circuit on 230 V has an 8 V drop. 8 ÷ 230 is about 0.035, and 0.035 × 100 = 3.5%. As a check, 1% of 230 V is 2.3 V, and 8 V is between three and four of those.

**Common mistakes**
- Dividing the wrong way round. 230 ÷ 8 counts how many 8 V pieces fit in 230 V, so put the part on top.
- Stopping at the decimal. 8 ÷ 230, about 0.035, is the share, and 0.035 × 100 = 3.5% is the percentage.
- Reading the part as the percentage. 30 m of a 40 m run is not 30%. It is 30 ÷ 40 × 100 = 75%.
- Dividing by the wrong whole. £50 of cable in a £200 order is 50 ÷ 200 = 25% of the order. Dividing by the £150 of fittings compares it with only the rest.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the part landing part ÷ whole of the way along the bar, with the whole lined up with 100%, when you divide the part by the whole and times by 100.

checks.label: Part ÷ whole × 100: 20 m of 50 m is 40%, 30 m of 40 m is 75%, 9 V of 230 V is about 3.9%, 25 A of 20 A is 125%, and every row of working on every screen holds, written with = only when exact and with ≈ when rounded (9 ÷ 230 ≈ 0.039, 230 ÷ 9 ≈ 25.6)

Each puzzle accepts only its own answer, part ÷ whole × 100 at the decimals shown, and every wrong answer offered is the one a named slip gives: the whole over the part, no times 100, ten times too big, the part read as a percentage, the difference, the smaller on top, the other share, the wrong whole
The slide puzzle accepts only 75% for 30 m of 40 m, opens with nothing placed, and gives 30% (the part read as a percentage) and 10% (the difference) their own hints

On the bar a percentage and its amount line up: the part lands at part ÷ whole of the way along, inside the bar when it is smaller than the whole and past its end when it is bigger (25 A on 20 A at 125%); 1% of 230 V is 2.3 V, so 9 V lands between 3% (6.9 V) and 4% (9.2 V)
Dividing the other way up counts pieces: 230 ÷ 9 = 25.6, so the bar takes 25 whole 9 V pieces with a bit left over, while one piece is 9 ÷ 230 × 100 = 3.9% of it
To change a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100: 0.67 × 100 = 67%, and in this lesson 0.4 is 40%, 0.75 is 75%, 0.039 is 3.9%, 0.026 is 2.6%, 0.035 is 3.5% and 1.25 is 125%
Per cent means out of 100, so the bar lined up with 100% is 100 equal hundredths of the whole: 40% of a 50 m drum is 20 m, and 1% of 230 V is 2.3 V
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends and its parts at least 0.5 s apart; every answer's motion within 2.5 s
The right answer moves between the three buttons: each place holds it on at least two of the seven puzzles, and no two puzzles in a row put it in the same place

Nothing pops in or out: painted every 1/60 s through every demonstration, and from the question through every right answer's motion to its finished picture, no part's opacity changes by more than 0.5 from one frame to the next

applied.problem: 9 ÷ 230 is 0.0391…, so writing "9 ÷ 230 = 0.039" gives a rounded figure as exact (false precision); the "about" belongs on the division, since 0.039 × 100 is exactly 3.9.
8 ÷ 230 is 0.0347…, so "8 ÷ 230 = 0.035" (twice) states a rounded value as exact; Dan's calculator will show 0.0347826…, so mark it as about 0.035.

notes.problem: Every entry has kind "constant", but 50 m, 40 m, 230 V drops of 9, 6 and 8 V, 24 circuits, 20 A, 2,000/1,500 W, 470 Ω and £150 are example amounts (assumed, as ignores says), and each percentage is computed from the shown rule; none is a fixed real-world value.

The course has no research.json, so the lesson cites nothing, though the research notes quote Electronics Tutorials (tolerance is "expressed as a percentage of its 'nominal' or preferred value") and NCETM ("Children view a percentage as a number rather than part of an amount") for points it teaches.

The worked example's lighting circuit with an 8 V drop (3.5%), like the 9 V drop (3.9%), is above the 3% the course opener says a lighting circuit is normally allowed, and nothing says so; once the limit is cited, say it is over, or use a circuit not held to 3%.
